text_blocks.snippet: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes high blood pressure in the lung arteries because the blood vessels have become narrowed, blocked, or destroyed, forcing the right side of the heart to work much harder.
snippet_highlighted_words: high blood pressure in the lung arteries

text_blocks.snippet: In the early stages, PAH may cause no noticeable symptoms at all. As it progresses, symptoms often mimic other heart or lung conditions, including:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical exertion like climbing stairs or walking, and eventually even at rest
Chest pain or pressure (angina), often triggered by activity
Heart palpitations (a racing or pounding heartbeat)

text_blocks.snippet: Advanced Symptoms (Signs of Right-Sided Heart Strain)
As the heart's right ventricle struggles to keep up with the elevated pressure, more severe signs can develop:

list.snippet: Swelling (edema) in the ankles, feet, legs, or abdomen (ascites) due to fluid retention
Fainting spells (syncope), particularly during or immediately after exercise
Coughing up blood (hemoptysis) in rare, advanced cases

text_blocks.snippet: Learn more about tracking warning signs through the American Lung Association.
If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, let me know:

list.snippet: Which specific symptoms are happening and how long they have lasted
Whether they occur mostly during activity or while resting

text_blocks.snippet: I can provide more information on what to expect or how doctors diagnose PAH.
